description_full: Griffon Corporation, through its subsidiaries, provides home and building, and consumer and professional products in the United States, Europe, Canada, Australia, and internationally. The Home and Building Products segment manufactures and markets residential and sectional commercial garage doors, rolling steel service doors, fire doors, shutters, steel security grilles, and room dividers. This segment also sells garage door openers. Its Consumer and Professional Products segment manufactures and markets long-handled engineered tools, including shovels, spades, scoops, rakes, hoes, cultivators, weeders, post hole diggers, scrapers, edgers, and forks; wheelbarrows and lawn carts; snow tools comprising pushers, roof rakes, sled sleigh shovels, and ice scrapers; and pruning products, such as pruners, loppers, shears, and other tools. This segment also offers striking tools, including axes, picks, mattocks, mauls, wood splitters, sledgehammers, pry bars, and repair handles; hand tools comprising hammers, screwdrivers, pliers, adjustable wrenches, handsaws, tape measures, levels, clamps, trowels, and other hand tools; indoor and outdoor planters and lawn accessories; and garden hoses and hose reels. In addition, this segment provides home organization products, including wire and wood shelving, containers, storage cabinets, and other closet and home organization accessories; residential, industrial, and commercial fans; and cleaning products, such as brooms, brushes, squeegees, and other cleaning products. It serves independent professional installing dealers and home center retail chains; and industrial distributors, homebuilders, and e-commerce platforms, as well as mass market, specialty, and hardware retailers. The company was formerly known as Instrument Systems Corporation and changed its name to Griffon Corporation in 1995. Griffon Corporation was incorporated in 1959 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Griffon Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.8B market cap on $2.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -4% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $305M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.99× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.3× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $101 (margin of safety -4%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 16%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $76.31 to $134 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 189% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.10).
It runs a 27% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 69% is amplified by 27.9x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.3x net debt to EBITDA ($99.0M of cash against $1.4B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.0% over 3 years, 0.9% over 5 years and 2.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 28.2% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 16% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 7%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 2.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 18.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 82%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (46 sales, net $23.5M sold).
It returns 4.6% a year to shareholders (3.8% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 4.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 22.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 5,100 employees, each generates about $494K of revenue, 1.4x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 2.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $60K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $9.5M (19x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
